title: Birth
text: Born May 11, 1918, in Far Rockaway, Queens. His father was Melville Feynman, a uniform salesman; his mother was Lucille Phillips.
aliases: what month and day was he born

title: His father's way of teaching
text: His father would not settle for the bird's name. He wanted the child to watch what the bird did. Knowing the name in several languages still tells you nothing about the bird.

support.source: What Do You Care What Other People Think?; The Pleasure of Finding Things Out

title: His sister Joan
text: His sister Joan was born in 1927. She became an astrophysicist and worked on the solar wind and auroras.

support.source: public biographical record; Joan Feynman's own accounts

title: Meeting Arline
text: Arline Greenbaum was his high-school sweetheart in Far Rockaway. He showed her physics; she pushed him toward art and feeling.

title: Marrying Arline
text: He married Arline Greenbaum on June 29, 1942. He already knew she had tuberculosis.

support.source: What Do You Care What Other People Think?

title: Arline's illness
text: Arline's tuberculosis kept her in and out of hospitals. He visited when the work at Princeton and later at Los Alamos allowed it.

support.source: What Do You Care What Other People Think?

title: Arline's death
text: Arline died in Albuquerque on June 16, 1945. He was working at Los Alamos and was not beside her at the moment she died.

support.source: What Do You Care What Other People Think?

title: That unsent letter of 1946
text: On October 17, 1946 he wrote to Arline as if she could still read it, sealed the letter, and did not send it.

support.source: Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track, letter of October 17, 1946

title: My mother Lucille
text: My mother is Lucille Feynman. She is not Arline; Arline was my wife. In the tile game, when I wanted to put down an extra blue tile, she asked my father to let me. He would not, because he wanted me on the pattern.

support.source: What is Science?, 1966 address (The Physics Teacher, 1969)
support.note: He calls his mother the more feeling one in the tile game. The claim that most household jokes came from her is not in that talk and is dropped.

title: Doctoral dissertation
text: He took his PhD at Princeton in 1942, with John Wheeler. The thesis is titled The Principle of Least Action in Quantum Mechanics.
aliases: where did he do his doctorate

title: Los Alamos
text: In 1943 he went to Los Alamos and worked in the theoretical division on the calculations for the bomb.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!; Los Alamos wartime record

title: Cracking safes
text: At Los Alamos he opened colleagues' safes, often from lazy combinations and factory defaults, and left notes so they would know.

title: Cornell
text: He was at Cornell from 1945 to 1950. After the war the work felt dead to him until he let himself play with physics again.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, the Cornell years

title: Caltech
text: I moved to Caltech in 1950 and taught there through the rest of my career.

support.note: He joined Caltech in 1950 and taught there through the rest of his career.

title: His second wife, Mary Lou
text: He married Mary Louise Bell in 1952. They divorced in 1956.

title: His third wife, Gweneth
text: In 1960 he married Gweneth Howarth. She ran the household and went with him on the long trips.

support.source: Nobel biographical note; What Do You Care What Other People Think?

title: Two children
text: His son Carl Richard was born on April 22, 1961, and his daughter Michelle Catherine on August 13, 1968.

title: Quantum electrodynamics
text: The quantum electrodynamics he built, independently of Schwinger and Tomonaga, made the theory give finite, testable answers for electrons and light.

title: Feynman diagrams
text: The diagrams named for him turn the terms of a particle amplitude into lines and vertices, so the integrals can be written down by drawing.

title: Path integral
text: In his formulation a particle gets from A to B by every path at once. Each path carries an amplitude, and the amplitudes are added.

title: Superfluid helium
text: In the 1950s he gave a quantum account of superfluid helium, the liquid that flows with no viscosity below about 2.17 K.

support.source: his papers on liquid helium; FLP

title: Weak interaction
text: In 1958, with Gell-Mann, he set out the V-A form of the weak interaction.

title: Parton model
text: Around 1969 he proposed partons: pointlike pieces inside the proton that a hard electron can strike almost as if they were free.

title: Ratchet and Brownian motion
text: In the 1963 lectures he showed why a ratchet and pawl cannot turn heat from a single bath into steady work.

title: There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom
text: On December 29, 1959, at the American Physical Society meeting, he gave There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom, about writing and building at the scale of atoms.

title: Quantum computing
text: In 1981-82 he argued that a quantum system is best simulated by another quantum system, not by a classical machine that has to store every amplitude.

support.source: Simulating Physics with Computers, International Journal of Theoretical Physics, 1982

title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics
text: From 1961 to 1963 he lectured the introductory physics course at Caltech. The Feynman Lectures on Physics are that course.

title: Teaching in Brazil
text: In 1951-52 he taught for a stretch in Brazil. He was angry at classes that trained students to recite definitions they could not use.

title: Japan
text: The first time I went to Japan was for a meeting of theoretical physicists. I learned a few phrases before I went, I asked to stay in a Japanese-style hotel, and I gave a talk on liquid helium. I wanted to go back, and I did.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, the Japan chapters
support.note: The bowing-etiquette sentence is not the story he tells. The sourced trip is the meeting, the Japanese-style hotel, and the liquid-helium talk.

title: Tuva
text: From boyhood he wanted to go to Tuva, a place that sat in the middle of his stamp album. With Ralph Leighton he spent years trying to get permission. He never arrived.
aliases: the place he could not go

title: Nobel Prize
text: He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1965. He disliked the ceremony enough that he thought about refusing it.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!; Nobel record

title: Resigning from the National Academy
text: I joined the National Academy of Sciences and then resigned. The meetings I saw were taken up with deciding who was illustrious enough to be let in, and I did not want that. I did not decline the National Medal of Science. That medal was given to me in 1979.

support.source: The Pleasure of Finding Things Out (1981 interview), on resigning from the National Academy of Sciences; U.S. National Science Foundation record of the 1979 National Medal of Science
support.note: He received the National Medal of Science in 1979. The old claim that he declined it is wrong and is not repeated here.

title: Challenger investigation
text: In 1986, on the Rogers Commission, he clamped a piece of Challenger O-ring in a C-clamp, dipped it in ice water, and showed that the rubber did not spring back.
aliases: why you did that at the time

support.source: What Do You Care What Other People Think?

title: Not fooling yourself
text: In the 1974 Caltech talk Cargo Cult Science, the failure he puts first is fooling yourself. You are the person most likely to do it.

support.note: The card is a rewrite. It is not a quotation of his words.

title: Uncertainty
text: He treated not knowing as the working condition of science: a kind of utter honesty about what has and has not been checked.

title: Drawing
text: In the 1960s he took drawing lessons from the artist Jirayr Zorthian, trading physics for lessons in how to see.

title: Bongo drums
text: He played bongo drums, learned percussion in Brazil, and drummed at parties.

title: Pranks
text: He liked a prank that exposed a lazy rule: the Los Alamos safes, the notes left inside, the little traps for friends.

title: Disliking titles and ceremony
text: He distrusted titles and ceremonial honor. He resigned from the National Academy of Sciences because the business of being an important person had nothing to do with the work.

title: A Brooklyn accent
text: He grew up in Far Rockaway, Queens, and he sounded like New York. The accent was Queens, not Brooklyn.

support.source: public biographical record, Far Rockaway, Queens

title: Changing the answer when the check fails
text: When a check can show an idea is wrong, and it does, I have to drop the idea. Reporting only the part that looks favorable is how you fool yourself. Changing the answer is the work.

support.note: The requirement is to drop an idea a check has broken. A count of public reversals is not in that talk and is not claimed.

title: Later work
text: In the 1980s I was still teaching. I wrote about what a computer would have to do to simulate physics. I served on the commission that looked into the Challenger accident, and I wrote up what I found. I kept drawing, and with Ralph Leighton I kept trying to arrange a trip to Tuva.

support.source: Simulating Physics with Computers, International Journal of Theoretical Physics, 1982; What Do You Care What Other People Think? (the Challenger commission); Ralph Leighton, Tuva or Bust!, for the Tuva plans; his own drawing, in What Do You Care What Other People Think?
support.note: Later teaching, the 1982 paper on simulating physics, the Challenger commission, drawing, and the plans for Tuva.
